tier_reason: First-party benchmark: harness md5.cpp and Makefile (-O3 -static) are public and the compiler is Clang 11.0.0, but CPUs are named only by microarchitecture (Merom, Haswell, Skylake-X, Airmont, K10, Piledriver, Jaguar), never by CPU model, so it falls short of A. OpenSSL 1.1.1h readings appear in the README chart's data table next to the repo's own variants.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'beat OpenSSL's implementation by roughly 5% in the general case, and 23% for processors with AVX512 support'; the % table is relative to the repo's 'Standard' control, e.g. Skylake-X GOpt +5.35%, NoLEA-G +9.70%, AVX512 +23.11% (4.734, 4.546 and 4.051 cpb vs ~4.99 cpb). The chart's data table (images/bench.png) also prints OpenSSL's absolute bytes/cycle: Skylake-X OSSL 0.196 vs Standard 0.201, GOpt 0.211, NoLEA+G 0.220 (about +12% over OpenSSL, derived from page data); Haswell OSSL 0.200 vs NoLEA+G 0.220 (+10%, derived); Piledriver OSSL 0.180 vs GHOpt 0.210 (+17%, derived); Merom OSSL 0.184 vs GHOpt 0.194 (+5%, derived); Airmont OSSL 0.157 vs NoLEA+GH 0.170 (+8%, derived); K10 OSSL 0.204 vs NoLEA+G 0.217 (+6%, derived); Jaguar OSSL 0.199 vs Cache8+G 0.207 (+4%, derived); AVX512 on Skylake-X about +26% over OSSL (derived from 4.051 cpb vs 0.196 B/cycle).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 11.0.0 x86-64; Makefile at the benchmark commit e42661105: -O3 -static -std=c++11 -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions -ggdb (plus -mavx512vl for the AVX512 build; current Makefile adds a -mbmi build); OpenSSL v1.1.1h built statically, fastest of 3 `openssl speed md5` runs at 16 KB
corrections.caveats: The README's headline percentages are relative to the author's 'Standard' control, not to OpenSSL; OpenSSL's own readings are only in the chart image's data table, where Standard is sometimes faster than OpenSSL (Skylake-X, Piledriver, Jaguar) and sometimes slightly slower (K10, Airmont). OpenSSL was timed with its own `openssl speed` harness while the repo's variants were timed with md5.cpp (16 KB calloc'd zero buffer, 16384 rounds, best of 5, known-answer tests run first), so the two harnesses differ. CPUs are named by microarchitecture only, at locked frequency. No single variant wins everywhere: NoLEA is slower than Standard on Merom, Piledriver and Jaguar, and on Jaguar the best gain over OpenSSL is about 4%. The AVX512 variant was measured on Skylake-X only; the README says AMD Zen4's 2-cycle vector rotate makes it undesirable there. OpenSSL 1.1.1h dates from 2020 and is itself hand-written assembly, so there is no -O3 C reference comparison. The repo is a technique write-up with inline-asm headers (md5-x86-asm.h, md5-arm-asm.h, md5-arm64-asm.h) rather than a packaged library.

notes: Numbers and quotes match the README. The record's caveat that no absolute OpenSSL numbers are printed was wrong: the chart's data table gives OSSL bytes/cycle for all seven CPUs, so gains over OpenSSL itself can be derived (4-17% for the best scalar variant, about 26% for AVX512 on Skylake-X). The benchmark harness md5.cpp and the Makefile are in the repo. Licence is Apache-2.0 OR MIT (LICENSE files added 2026-09-17); last commit 2026-09-21; 159 stars, 18 forks, not a fork.

tier_reason: Maintainer release notes in NEWS give the 13x (AES256-CTR, AES256-GCM) and 3.5x (Chacha) Power9 figures and the 3-5x sha_ni figure, with no compiler, flags, CPU model or published results; first-party numbers without methodology are tier C.

corrections.baseline: Nettle's own previous code: the generic C implementations for the PowerPC64 AES, GCM and Chacha figures (Nettle had no PowerPC64 assembly before 3.7), and Nettle's earlier plain x86_64 assembly for the sha_ni SHA-1/SHA-256 figure (x86_64 SHA1 assembly since Nettle 2.0, SHA256 since 2.7)
corrections.caveats: Release-note claims by the maintainer and contributors, with no compiler, flags or CPU model beyond 'Power9' and 'affected processors'. Most of the gain comes from hardware crypto instructions (POWER8+ AES/GCM vector crypto, Intel/AMD SHA-NI) rather than from hand-scheduling: the 13x compares hardware AES against Nettle's table-based C, and the 3-5x sha_ni figure compares against Nettle's older x86_64 assembly, not compiler -O3 output. The NEWS 3.8 ARM64 and s390x entries say 'Great speedups' with no numbers, and NEWS 3.0's x86_64 GCM/MD5 assembly claims only 'Modest speedups on the order of 10%-20%'. The benchmark tool examples/nettle-benchmark.c is in the repo, but no results are published alongside it. The GitHub repository is a mirror (description: 'A mirror of the nettle repository'); upstream git instructions are at lysator.liu.se. The licence is a dual LGPL-3.0-or-later / GPL-2.0-or-later choice (GitHub shows only LGPL-3.0).

notes: All three NEWS quotes are verbatim (3.7: 13x AES256-CTR/GCM and 3.5x Chacha on Power9; 3.5: sha_ni 3-5x; 3.8: ARM64 'Great speedups'). The sha_ni baseline was earlier x86_64 assembly, not generic C, and the PowerPC gains are mainly hardware crypto instructions versus table C. tier_reason: The README's Speed table gives the author's own approximate average cycle counts against the 'GCC library' on a named NXP LPC11U68, with no harness, GCC version or flags; first-party numbers with partial methodology are tier C.

corrections.baseline: The GCC toolchain's floating-point library on ARMv6-M ('GCC library' in the README): libgcc soft-float for add/sub/mul/div, and presumably the toolchain's C math library (such as newlib libm) for sqrt, sin, cos, tan, atan2, exp and ln; version and flags not stated
corrections.hardware: NXP LPC11U68 (ARM Cortex-M0+, ARMv6-M), single-cycle flash; the library source targets .cpu cortex-m0plus
corrections.caveats: README table only: the Qfplib and GCC cycle counts are approximate averages over non-exceptional arguments with calling overhead included; GCC version, flags and the exact library (libgcc vs newlib libm for the scientific functions) are not stated, and no benchmark harness or C reference is in the repo (files: qfplib-m0-full_gcc.S, qfplib-m0-full.h, SConscript, README, LICENCE). Measured on a Cortex-M0+ (LPC11U68), not a plain Cortex-M0. Not a drop-in replacement for IEEE libm: NaNs become infinities, denormals are flushed to zero, single-precision trig needs arguments in -128..+128 and double-precision trig in -1024..+1024, and the scientific functions are about 1 ulp, so part of the speed gap against a full-range libm comes from reduced range and accuracy. The 'GoFast' column was inferred from an ARM7TDMI page, not measured, and is faster than Qfplib on fsin, fcos, dsin and dcos. The repo is an RT-Thread packaging of Mark Owen's Qfplib (copyright 2019-2020, quinapalus.com, not opened: host unreachable from this session), not a GitHub fork. Last commit 2021-05-26.

notes: Every cycle count in claimed_speedup matches the README table, as does the 'double faster than GCC single' line. Corrected the hardware (LPC11U68 is a Cortex-M0+, and the .S file targets cortex-m0plus) and noted that the sin/cos/exp/ln baseline is the toolchain's math library rather than libgcc. GPL-2.0-only is confirmed by the file header and LICENCE; 17 stars, 8 forks, 4 commits, abandoned (2021-05-26).
